extracted.intended_audience: Presbyterian ministers, church officers, and informed congregants engaged in ecclesiastical-political debate about the lawfulness of civil magistracy
extracted.subtask_description: Articulating the scriptural and constitutional standards that determine who is a lawful magistrate and how civil authority ought to be constituted and recognized under divine law. The text evaluates qualifications, the role of divine precept vs. providence, and the legitimacy of popular consent and oaths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural qualifications for magistrates (Exod. xviii.21 etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates must be 'able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness' (Exod. xviii.21); a person 'in whom is the spirit' (Numb. xxvii.18); 'wise men and understanding, and known among your tribes' (Deut. i.13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These texts are treated as plain, positive, moral precepts that demonstrate what magistrates ought to be: capable, fearing God, truthful, not covetous, possessing the spirit of wisdom/government, known for integrity and understanding. The author emphasizes negatives (not children, not fools) and positives (known affection to the people's real welfare).

rubrics_metrics.name: King must be of God's choosing / not a stranger (Deut. xvii.14-15)
rubrics_metrics.description: When setting a king the people are limited to 'one from among thy brethren' whom 'the Lord thy God shall choose'; one must not set a stranger over them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This precept is read expansively: 'brother' refers especially to religious affinity, not merely kinship or nationality. The ruler must not be a stranger or enemy to true religion; he should be expected to advance the kingdom of Jesus Christ. The choice of magistrate is thereby circumscribed by God's direction and not left to unfettered popular will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice and godly fear as essential attributes (2 Sam. xxiii; Job xxxiv)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ruler 'must be just, ruling in the fear of God' and one 'that hateth right should not govern.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulership must be exercised in justice and godly fear; rulers who 'hate right' or are ungodly are disqualified. Biblical speakers (Davidic/prophetic) are cited to support the ethical demands upon officeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural qualifications are essential to the being/validity of magistracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualifications stated in Scripture are not merely advantageous to usefulness but are necessary to the very being and validity of the magistrate's office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text rejects the claim that qualifications only affect a magistrate's usefulness. If qualifications are essential to the office's proper ends, then they are essential to its being; otherwise the ordinance would be useless and divine wisdom would be contradicted. The author uses analogy to ministry qualifications (Tit. i; 1 Tim. iii) to show equal peremptoriness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity of magistrate and minister qualifications/authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The qualifications for magistrates are required in the same express and strong terms as those for ministers (Tit. i; 1 Tim. iii); both offices are clothed with authority from the law of God and require subjection and obedience under the same pains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Scripture requires similar qualifications for both offices, one must not treat magistracy as less exacting than ministry. The author argues against a double standard that would tolerate unqualified civil rulers while demanding more of ecclesiastical officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain distinction between preceptive and providential will of God
rubrics_metrics.description: A necessary distinction exists between God's preceptive (what he commands) and providential (what he permits/happens) will; conflating them leads to uncertainty about duty and legitimizes opposing God's precepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providence may serve as commentary but is not a rule of duty where Scripture is silent; where Scripture ordains, providence gives no relaxation. Overthrowing this distinction would make providence a rule equal to the written word, undermine revelation, and justify actions (including rebellion) merely because they succeed providentially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providential possession does not equal approbative divine ordination
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that someone is raised by providence or acknowledged by people does not demonstrate God's approbation or confer a lawful title to office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providence cannot, by itself, discover God's allowance or confer approbation; lawful title requires conformity to the preceptive will (Scripture). Accepting providential rise as preceptive would license robbery, fraud, and every usurpation under the pretense of 'providence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil consent alone is insufficient to constitute lawful magistracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil society's inclinations and consent, if made the sole basis of civil power, would legitimize magistrates contrary to God's preceptive law and exalt creaturely will above the Creator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly condemns the 'anti-scriptural' tenet that consent alone makes a magistrate lawful, arguing it undermines divine ordinances, dissolves scriptural qualifications, and leads to anarchy and the legitimizing of wicked rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uphold fundamental laws/constitutions and prescribed qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations commonly enact fundamental laws, constitutions, and provisos (e.g., excluding Papists from the British throne) that fence the throne and make certain qualifications essential; these are legitimate and consistent with Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such human securities serve to prevent admission of unqualified persons and to preserve covenant/reformation principles. The author argues historical practice and positive constitutions (e.g., post-revolution settlement) confirm that qualifications beyond mere popular will may rightly be made essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oaths of allegiance and covenant obligations should be reconciled to lawful government
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegiance to a lawful government (as recognized by civil society and providence) is a duty owed by subjects and can be reconciled with covenantal oaths; refusing to swear allegiance while acknowledging a government's lawfulness is inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text critiques 'Seceders' who refuse to swear allegiance on the grounds that it homologates an undesired constitution. The guidance is that allegiance binds one to own the lawfulness of the government and to maintain it according to its constitution; if covenants forbid certain duties, that forbiddance should be shown, not simply asserted as incompatible.
